clinicalPearls: Typically arises in the first two decades, presenting with progressive pain and swelling in the metaphysis of long bones or the posterior elements of the spine
Imaging shows an expansile, eccentric, multiloculated lytic lesion with a thin shell of bone and characteristic fluid-fluid levels on MRI or CT
Fluid-fluid levels reflect sedimentation of uncoagulated blood within cystic spaces and are suggestive but not pathognomonic
Primary lesions harbour USP6 gene rearrangement, distinguishing them from a secondary ABC-like change occurring within another tumour
Always exclude a secondary aneurysmal bone cyst arising in giant cell tumour, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma or a telangiectatic osteosarcoma before diagnosing a primary lesion
Standard management is intralesional curettage with bone grafting or adjuncts, though sclerotherapy and selective embolisation are increasingly used
Local recurrence after curettage is not uncommon, particularly with incomplete removal in young children
reference.pathophysiology: Aneurysmal bone cyst is a benign but locally destructive neoplasm composed of blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septa containing osteoclast-type giant cells, reactive woven bone and spindle cells. Primary lesions are driven by rearrangement of the USP6 gene, which places the coding sequence under an active promoter and drives cell proliferation, confirming a true neoplastic rather than purely reactive process. Expansion of the vascular spaces thins and remodels the surrounding cortex, producing the expansile appearance and structural weakening. A morphologically identical secondary process can be superimposed on other primary bone tumours, which lack the USP6 rearrangement.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour of bone with secondary cystic change
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiography to characterise the expansile lytic pattern and cortical shell
MRI to demonstrate fluid-fluid levels and internal septation and assess soft-tissue extension
CT for cortical detail and pre-operative planning, particularly in the spine and pelvis
Biopsy with histological confirmation to exclude a malignant mimic before definitive treatment
Molecular testing for USP6 rearrangement to confirm a primary lesion when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rapid growth, a permeative margin or an associated soft-tissue mass suggesting telangiectatic osteosarcoma
Spinal lesions causing neurological compromise or vertebral instability
Pathological fracture through a weakened expanded cortex
Recurrence with more aggressive imaging features after prior treatment
reference.prognosis: Primary aneurysmal bone cyst is benign and does not metastasise, with generally good outcomes after complete removal, although local recurrence occurs in a minority and repeat treatment may be needed. Outcome depends heavily on excluding a malignant mimic at the outset.
pitfalls: Mistaking a telangiectatic osteosarcoma for a benign aneurysmal bone cyst on imaging alone
Diagnosing a primary lesion without excluding a secondary aneurysmal change within another tumour
Assuming fluid-fluid levels are specific, as they occur in several cystic bone lesions
Underestimating recurrence risk after incomplete curettage in skeletally immature patients

management: Confirm the diagnosis with biopsy before definitive treatment, since telangiectatic osteosarcoma can mimic ABC on imaging, unless an experienced bone tumour service is monitoring characteristic imaging closely

Distinguish primary ABC (USP6 gene rearrangement, a true neoplasm) from secondary ABC arising within another bone tumour such as giant cell tumour, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, or telangiectatic osteosarcoma, since secondary cases are managed by treating the underlying lesion
Treat confirmed primary ABC with local control measures rather than systemic therapy; chemotherapy and radiotherapy have no established first-line role in uncomplicated lesions

Consider observation for small, asymptomatic, incidentally found lesions in non-critical locations; treat actively when there is structural risk such as cortical thinning, growth plate involvement, spinal instability, or pathological fracture risk
Use intralesional curettage combined with bone grafting or a bone-void filler as first-line surgical treatment for accessible lesions

Consider percutaneous sclerotherapy as a primary alternative to surgery or as an adjunct, particularly for spinal or pelvic lesions or in young children where extensive surgery carries higher morbidity
Use selective arterial embolisation pre-operatively to reduce bleeding in highly vascular lesions, or as a standalone or repeated strategy in surgically difficult spinal or pelvic lesions
Reserve en bloc resection for lesions not amenable to curettage or refractory to repeated intralesional treatment, weighing the greater functional cost

Consider off-label denosumab, targeting osteoclast-type giant cells, only for refractory or surgically inaccessible disease and only through a specialist bone tumour board, with attention to RANKL inhibition class effects; specific dosing decisions belong in a structured protocol
Do not use radiotherapy routinely, given the benign nature of the disease and long-term radiation risk in a typically young population
Reserve systemic or anti-resorptive therapy for refractory, surgically inaccessible disease managed by a specialist bone tumour service

Monitor after treatment with serial plain radiographs and MRI as needed to assess healing of the curettage cavity or resolution after sclerotherapy or embolisation, continuing follow-up for a period to detect recurrence, which is not uncommon particularly in young children
Extend clinical and radiographic follow-up in skeletally immature patients with growth plate involvement to monitor for growth disturbance

Refer to an orthopaedic oncology or bone tumour service before biopsy or treatment for suspected ABC with atypical imaging, spinal or pelvic location, or possible malignant mimicry, and refer urgently for spinal lesions with instability or neurological compromise
